messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ahmed, a forty‑year‑old paramedic of Lebanese descent, had always prided himself on the steadiness of his hands and the calm of his mind on the ambulance bay. His wife, Mariam, and their two children keep the house humming, but the quiet of their home has become a backdrop to a growing unease. In March, when he was called to a three‑story residential fire, the tragedy that unfolded there would haunt him for years. A burst pipe had turned the living room into a maze of slick concrete and falling timber. He found his younger brother, Karim, trapped under a collapsed sofa, blood gushing from a shattered rib cage. Ahmed’s first instinct was to extricate him, but the fire’s heat and the smell of burning wood overwhelmed his efforts. He pulled Karim to a shallow safety zone, but the boy’s eyes had already gone dim. The paramedics who arrived later took Karim to the emergency department, the antiseptic scent of the hospital lingering as he watched the ambulance door shut behind him. He had failed to save him. That day left Ahmed with a constellation of sensations: the sight of visible injuries on a loved one, the sharp, metallic taste of antiseptic, and the memory of the boy’s last breath. Whenever he now passes by a casualty ward, the visual reminder of a wounded body triggers a flood of terror. The mere sight of a wound, the whiff of antiseptic, or even the flash of a blood‑stained bandage sets his heart racing. The triggers ignite his maladaptive strategies—he suppresses the thought of that day, overworks at the station to keep his mind on the next call, and avoids any patient or scene that might resemble his brother’s injuries. He no longer attends mandatory training sessions, citing exhaustion. The visual cues also heighten his threat reactions: a sudden touch from a colleague’s hand sends him flinching as if a blade were behind it, and he insists on choosing the most “secure” seats in meetings, preferring the back corner where he feels protected. The same triggers summon vivid sensory memories of the fire, causing him to relive every crackling flame, every splintering splinter of wood, as though it were the present. In these moments, he experiences the terror of that night again, the same primal fear he felt when the house was still ablaze. The memories, in turn, reinforce Ahmed’s negative appraisals. Each intrusive recollection confirms that he is permanently damaged, that he can no longer trust himself to act when danger is present. The guilt that his brother’s life could have been saved feels like a permanent scar on his conscience, a failure that he cannot shake. These appraisals drive him further into avoidance and overwork. Believing he has failed, he tries to compensate by working harder, hoping that relentless effort will prove his worth. Yet, the more he works, the more his mind is forced to suppress the past, and the more his startle responses become frequent, even to benign touches. The fear of being hurt again amplifies his sensitivity to any trigger—an accidental glance at a wound, the echo of a hospital corridor, the faint smell of antiseptic. Each of these cues pulls him deeper into a cycle of avoidance, threat, and memory that feels impossible to escape. When Ahmed’s coworkers notice he sits alone at the break room, he attributes it to his need for safety, but in reality, the avoidance is a response to the trigger of visual injuries and the threat of sudden contact. The avoidance itself feeds his memory intrusions: the isolation forces his mind to replay the scene, to imagine the crack of a splinter in the back of a hospital bed. The reliving, with its full sensory detail, increases his sense of failure and makes him feel even more incapable. Overworking, intended to keep his mind busy, paradoxically creates space for the intrusive images, because each pause is an invitation for the memory to surface. The threat reactions—being startled by a touch or losing concentration—are not just reactions to the present; they are amplified by the sense that his body is still in a state of emergency, always on guard. Every time he feels a threat, his self‑efficacy erodes further, reinforcing the belief that he cannot rely on himself. His belief that he failed to protect his brother makes him more attuned to potential threats; he scans the ambulance bay for anything that might resemble a dangerous scene, even when none is present. Thus, his maladaptive strategies, memory, threat, and negative appraisals are locked together, each pulling the other into a tightening loop that leaves him exhausted, paranoid, and increasingly isolated. The cycle has taken a toll on Ahmed’s life. He no longer volunteers for night shifts, fearing the possibility of an emergency involving a wounded loved one. His wife, concerned, has urged him to see a therapist, but Ahmed has resisted, convinced that staying in the field will prove his worth. Yet the relentless cycle of avoidance and overwork has made his work performance slip, and he has missed key procedural updates. The fear that he might again fail, combined with the knowledge that his avoidance is harming his career, is what finally pushes him to seek help. Ahmed now stands at a crossroad: he hopes to reclaim a sense of control over his body’s reactions, to trust himself again, and to stop fearing that one more glance at a wound will bring back the terror of that night. He is terrified that the cycle will persist, that he will continue to be unable to rely on himself, and that his sense of permanent damage will never ease. In his own words, he longs for a way to stop being haunted by his brother’s death and to find a space where he can function without the constant, paralyzing threat that haunts every trigger.
